extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, educated readers, and scholars evaluating writers, critics, and social/political argumentation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the quality, honesty, method, and style of writers and literary critics (illustrated by discussion of Malthus and Gifford). Focuses on argumentative premises, use of evidence, style, intellectual independence, and political or moral implications of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate attribution and acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Malthus 'has borrowed (perhaps without consciousness, at any rate without acknowledgment) both the preliminary statement ... and the subsequent use made of this statement' from Wallace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars should acknowledge sources; failing to credit origins undermines intellectual honesty and can mislead readers about originality. Anti-pattern: presenting another's ideas as one's own or obscuring provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and parity of premises/analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: He premises these two propositions as the basis of all his reasoning, I. That food is necessary to man; 2. That the desire to propagate the species is an equally indispensable law of our existence: — thus making it appear that these two wants or impulses are equal and coordinate principles of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether foundational premises are actually comparable. Beware false analogies (e.g., treating hunger and sexual passion as equally imperative). If premises are false or incomparable, subsequent reasoning may collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper recognition of moral restraint as a check
rubrics_metrics.description: He now says that moral restraint is to be coupled with these [vice and misery], and that its influence depends greatly on the state of laws and manners — and Utopia stands where it did, a great way off indeed, but not turned topsy-turvy by our magician's wand!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether moral, cultural, and institutional factors (habit, resolution, public opinion) are adequately considered as restraints or modifiers of broad laws. Anti-pattern: dismissing moral restraint as 'very inconsiderable, or none at all' without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of dramatization and exaggerated statements
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to produce something of a startling and dramatic effect, he has strained a point or two. In order to quell and frighten away the bugbear of Modern Philosophy, he was obliged to make a sort of monster of the principle of population...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists should not overstate or dramatize conclusions to gain rhetorical effect. Exaggeration can mislead policy and public opinion; prefer measured, balanced claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against mathematical over-simplification in social theory
rubrics_metrics.description: He attempted ... in giving to the disproportionate power of increase in the principle of population and the supply of food a mathematical form, or reducing it to the arithmetical and geometrical ratios, in which we believe Mr. Malthus is now generally admitted ... to have been wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mechanically impose arithmetic/geometric laws on complex social phenomena without empirical basis. Check whether claimed ratios hold across contexts; beware of treating a mathematical model as a universal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'laws of nature' from laws of human arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of nature, to which the author appeals, are no other than a limited fertility and a limited earth. Within those bounds, the rest is regulated by the laws of man. The division of the produce of the soil, the price of labour, the relief afforded to the poor, are matters of human arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking 'natural' limits, critics must separate physical constraints from contingent human institutions and policies. Policy recommendations should account for what is socially or legally changeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid political or partisan servility and pandering
rubrics_metrics.description: He wished not merely to advance ... certain great and valuable truths, but at the same time to overthrow certain unfashionable paradoxes by exaggerated statements — to curry favour with existing prejudices and interests by garbled representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and critics should avoid tailoring arguments to please parties or interests. Watch for garbled representations or selective emphasis intended to win favor rather than seek truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and tone: correctness, elegance, and civility
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Malthus's style is correct and elegant; his tone of controversy mild and gentlemanly; and the care with which he has brought his facts and documents together, deserves the highest praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, correct, and civil expression, plus careful documentation, are virtues in argumentative writing. Good style supports credibility and persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligent assembly and use of facts and documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The care with which he has brought his facts and documents together, deserves the highest praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the thoroughness and accuracy of evidence-gathering. Well-supported claims require sensible, transparent use of data and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh sense over mere grammar or technical pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: In studying an old author, he has no notion of any thing beyond adjusting a point, proposing a different reading, or correcting, by the collation of various copies, an error of the press. In appreciating a modern one, if it is an enemy, the first thing he thinks of is to charge him with bad grammar — he scans his sentences instead of weighing his sense;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should prioritize meaning, argument, and artistic effect rather than merely enumerating mechanical errors. Anti-pattern: fixating on trivial editorial mistakes while ignoring substantive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid petty, captious, and literal criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing liberal, nothing humane in his style of judging: it is altogether petty, captious, and literal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good criticism is generous, broad-minded, and humane. Avoid nitpicking that misses an author's intent or larger accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual independence; do not be subservient to power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor's political subserviency adds the last finishing to his ridiculous pedantry and vanity. He has all his life been a follower in the train of wealth and power — strives to back his pretensions ... by a place at court, and to gild his reputation ... by the smile of greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should resist aligning judgment with political or social power. Independence preserves integrity; beware of flattering authorities for advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to novelty; do not insist on classical uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: He believes that modern literature should wear the fetters of classical antiquity; that truth is to be weighed in the scales of opinion and prejudice; that power is equivalent to right; that genius is dependent on rules;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid demanding that contemporary works strictly conform to antiquated forms or rules. Recognize legitimate innovation in form, diction, and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from using personal circumstances as grounds for literary condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: He travails his adversaries ... with some personal or accidental defect. If a writer has been punished for a political libel, he is sure to hear of it in a literary criticism. If a lady goes on crutches and is out of favour at court, she is reminded of it in Mr. Gifford's manly satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fair criticism addresses the work, not the author's unrelated misfortunes or social standing. Using personal facts to discredit a work is an unfair advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not gatekeep literary merit by education or rank
rubrics_metrics.description: To edge into the Quarterly ... the candidate must have a diploma from the Universities, a passport from the Treasury. Otherwise, it is a breach of etiquette to let him pass, an insult to the better sort who aspire to the love of letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works on their intrinsic merits, not the author's pedigree or official endorsements. Avoid exclusionary practices that privilege rank over talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to flashes of thought and flights of fancy, not condemn them as disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Flashes of thought, flights of fancy, idiomatic expressions, he sets down among the signs of the times — the extraordinary occurrences of the age we live in. They are marks of a restless and revolutionary spirit: they disturb his composure of mind, and threaten (by implication) the safety of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should recognize and value imaginative risks and originality rather than dismissing them as mere symptoms of disorder. Innovation can signal vitality in literature.
